strengths: Addresses an important and underconstrained problem: metric-scale amodal 3D reconstruction under severe hand occlusion for robotic manipulation, where vision alone is insufficient.
The multimodal formulation fusing egocentric RGB, proprioception, and multi-contact touch in a shared camera-aligned SDF grid is technically sound and well motivated.
The architecture combining a Structure-VAE, conditional flow matching, and decoder-based physics guidance is clearly presented and builds sensibly on recent generative 3D representations.
Simulation experiments show improvements over Amodal3R and SAM3D, especially in higher-occlusion bins, and pose estimation benefits substantially from proprioception and tactile constraints.
Real-robot validation on a humanoid with an unseen end-effector provides valuable evidence of cross-embodiment transfer and practical applicability.
Ablations on sensing modalities and tactile-noise robustness are included, and the limitations section candidly discusses calibration, resolution, and generalization constraints.
weaknesses: Although physical plausibility is the central claim, the paper lacks quantitative metrics for contact consistency, non-interpenetration, penetration volume, or contact alignment; physical validity is supported mainly qualitatively.
The ablation does not isolate the effect of inference-time physics guidance versus the training-time contact/non-interpenetration losses, so the contribution of decoder guidance is not quantified.
Novelty is somewhat incremental: the method builds heavily on existing SDF/flow/amodal 3D generation pipelines, with the main additions being multimodal conditioning and physics losses.

Evaluation is limited: simulation uses synthetic grasp scenes and a subset of YCB, while real-world experiments cover only five objects and do not control for end-effector identity; baselines are also trained on different and often larger datasets, making comparisons not fully apples-to-apples.

Reproducibility is not fully demonstrated: key hyperparameters (latent dimension, loss weights, guidance parameters, training schedule, exact grasp generation details) are not all specified in the main paper, and code release is not indicated.

The baseline table contains a likely typo (SAM3D B3 NC = 0.081), and the proposed method does not improve all metrics over SAM3D in simulation (e.g., F@0.02), which weakens the claim of uniform physical-constraint gains.
Stage B is described as optional and minimally adapted, but its benefit is not evaluated in detail, so the downstream textured-reconstruction claim is only weakly substantiated.

The method relies on accurate hand-camera calibration, forward kinematics, and reliable occlusion masks; the real-world analysis shows sensitivity to calibration noise, which limits practical deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: amodal 3D object reconstruction under severe hand occlusion for robotic manipulation.
The multimodal formulation fusing RGB, proprioception, and tactile contact in a shared camera-aligned SDF grid is conceptually appealing and well motivated.

The method integrates physically motivated contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses into both training and inference-time guidance, which is a reasonable direction for physically grounded generative reconstruction.
The proposed camera-aligned, pose-aware SDF representation and Structure-VAE/flow-matching pipeline are described clearly enough to understand the intended architecture.
The authors include large-scale synthetic training data, evaluation on a YCB subset, and a real-robot deployment, demonstrating feasibility on hardware.
The limitations section acknowledges calibration sensitivity, fixed grid resolution, and uncertain generalization to new hands/sensors, which is useful.
weaknesses: The main quantitative claims are overstated. In Table 1, the paper states that its method improves all metrics except F@0.02 in the least-occluded regime, but SAM3D actually achieves higher F@0.02 on B1, B2, B3, B4, and All (e.g., All: SAM3D 0.228 vs. Ours 0.189). This materially weakens the claimed superiority.

The ablation evidence appears inconsistent. In Table A1, the No-Touch variant has NC, F@0.02, Voxel IoU, and EMD values exactly identical to the full model across all occlusion bins, differing only in CD (e.g., B1 No-Touch NC 0.868, F 0.215, IoU 0.616, EMD 0.158), which is highly implausible if touch is removed. This raises serious concerns about the validity of the ablation study.

Additional inconsistencies further undermine confidence: the Vision-Only F@0.02 bin values in Table A1 match Amodal3R’s bin values exactly while the All value differs, and the main text reports 22,680 YCB test images whereas the supplementary material reports 20,760 rendered YCB images (865 grasps x 24 views).

The paper’s central physical-plausibility claims are not quantitatively evaluated. There are no reported metrics for hand-object interpenetration volume, contact distance/alignment, or physical feasibility rate, despite these being core contributions. Qualitative examples alone are inadequate.

Stage B is presented as important for textured/refined reconstruction, but it is not quantitatively evaluated. The abstract and contributions imply a complete textured reconstruction pipeline, yet the experiments essentially assess Stage A geometry only.

The metric-scale claim is not convincingly supported. Evaluation appears to be performed in normalized/canonical SDF grids, random in-grid similarity transforms are used during training, and no explicit scale-error metric is reported. This makes the “correct real-world scale” claim difficult to verify.

Key ablations are missing or conflated. The paper does not isolate the effects of the non-interpenetration loss, contact loss, and inference-time decoder guidance relative to each other, nor does it clearly separate gains from touch, proprioception, and physics-based losses.

The real-world evidence is limited and sometimes mischaracterized. Only five YCB objects are tested, pose estimation is not quantitatively evaluated on the real robot, and the text calls the real-world performance “slightly lower” even though the method is better on CD, NC, and Voxel IoU but worse on F@0.02 and EMD.

The cross-embodiment generalization claim is not adequately supported. Only one real robot hand is tested, no per-end-effector quantitative comparison is provided, and the supplementary material admits end-effector identity is not isolated as a controlled variable.

Important implementation and reproducibility details are missing or unclear: hyperparameters such as λ_L1, λ_eik, λ_n, λ_KL, λ_NI, λ_C, β, η, α, and latent resolution R′ are not fully specified, nor are architecture sizes, training schedules, and random seeds. There are also section-numbering errors (e.g., “4.2.2” under the Method section) and a likely typo in Table 1 (SAM3D B3 NC = 0.081).

The evaluation protocol may be biased by considering only valid output meshes without reporting the invalid/failure rate. This can hide failure modes and make methods that produce more invalid meshes appear stronger than they are.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: amodal 3D reconstruction under severe hand occlusion, where vision alone is fundamentally ambiguous. It proposes a novel and sensible use of proprioception and multi-contact touch as geometric constraints in a generative reconstruction pipeline.

The pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation in the same 3D grid as the posed hand is technically sound. It enables metric-scale reconstruction, implicit object pose estimation, and differentiable physical constraints such as contact consistency and non-interpenetration.

The physics-based objectives are integrated thoughtfully into both finetuning and inference via decoder-guided sampling. This is a principled way to steer generation toward physically plausible shapes, not merely a post-hoc filtering step.

The empirical study is broad for this setting: simulation experiments over 36 YCB objects with occlusion-level stratification, ablation of sensing modalities, tactile-noise robustness tests, and real-robot transfer to an unseen end-effector. Results generally support the claim that proprioception and touch improve completion and pose estimation under high occlusion.
The paper is clear about its limitations, including calibration sensitivity, fixed grid resolution, and limited generalization across embodiments, which strengthens the scientific assessment.
The method integrates naturally into existing two-stage shape-appearance pipelines, making it potentially useful for downstream robotic manipulation tasks.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the framework builds heavily on existing components such as SDF VAEs, flow matching, TRELLIS/SLat-style pipelines, and Amodal3R-style occlusion-aware conditioning. The main contribution is the multimodal conditioning and physics losses rather than a fundamentally new generative formulation.

The baselines are not fully controlled. SAM3D and Amodal3R are trained with larger datasets and/or model capacity, and SAM3D is given ground-truth depth for pose estimation, while the proposed method relies on proprioception and touch. This makes the comparison informative but not entirely apples-to-apples.

Real-world validation is limited to five YCB objects on one humanoid platform with one unseen end-effector. This is useful but insufficient to strongly substantiate broad cross-embodiment or real-world generalization claims.

Stage B is presented as an integration step, but there is little quantitative evaluation of the final textured/refined reconstruction. The abstract and pipeline suggest more than the experiments actually demonstrate about downstream appearance and refinement.

There are some clarity/reproducibility concerns in the tables and text. For example, Table 1 reports SAM3D B3 NC as 0.081, which appears inconsistent with the rest of its results; Table 2 aggregate values are not simple averages and need clearer weighting explanation; and the real-world text says performance is slightly lower while the proposed method is better on several metrics in Table 3.

The inference-time physics guidance introduces additional computation and hyperparameters (guidance strength, decay, trust region), but the cost and sensitivity are not quantified. The dependence on accurate camera-hand calibration and tactile-to-surface mapping is acknowledged but not fully analyzed.

The paper does not compare against other vision-touch reconstruction methods, partially because the setting differs, but this leaves open how much the specific choice of multimodal flow model matters relative to alternative fusion strategies.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-explored problem: metric-scale amodal 3D object reconstruction under severe hand occlusion for robotic manipulation, where vision alone is fundamentally underconstrained. Integrating proprioception and multi-contact touch as geometric constraints is a well-motivated direction.

The technical formulation is mostly clear and coherent: a pose-aware, camera-aligned SDF representation, a Structure-VAE latent space, conditional flow matching, physics-based training losses (contact consistency and non-interpenetration), and differentiable decoder guidance at inference. The overall pipeline is described in sufficient detail for an expert reader to understand the main components.

The ablation study is informative and supports the central claim that touch and proprioception complement vision. It isolates vision-only, no-touch, tactile representation choices, training physics losses, inference guidance, and robustness to mask/kinematic/tactile noise.

The simulation results show clear improvements over the vision-only Amodal3R baseline and generally favorable results against SAM3D on several metrics, especially Voxel IoU and pose estimation. The occlusion-stratified evaluation is useful for understanding where multimodal physical cues help most.

The real-world transfer experiment on a humanoid robot with an end-effector different from those used in training is a valuable practical contribution. It demonstrates non-trivial cross-embodiment applicability and includes qualitative examples of contact- and penetration-related corrections.

The method integrates naturally into existing two-stage shape/appearance pipelines, such as SLAT-style refinement or SAM3D refinement, and preserves metric scale and pose. This makes the contribution practically relevant beyond a standalone reconstruction model.

The paper includes meaningful limitations and societal/robotic deployment considerations, especially regarding calibration sensitivity, fixed grid resolution, and failure cases under hand-object misalignment.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental. The approach builds heavily on existing components: TRELLIS/SLAT-style latent 3D generation, Amodal3R-style occlusion conditioning, flow matching, and standard SDF/physics regularization. The main new elements are the tactile/proprioceptive conditioning and physics-guided fine-tuning/inference, which are useful but not deeply architectural.

The main comparison against SAM3D is not fully controlled. SAM3D is a larger model trained on much larger datasets, and for pose estimation the authors compare against a best-case SAM3D using ground-truth depth. Conversely, the paper's own vision-only variant is only in the ablation, not in the main comparison table. A controlled same-architecture, same-data comparison would better isolate the benefit of proprioception and touch.

Some claims about experimental results are inaccurate or overstated. In Table 1, SAM3D has better F@0.02 overall and in B1-B4 (equal in B4), not only in the least-occluded regime. In Table 3, the proposed method has worse F@0.02 and EMD than SAM3D, so the real-world statement that the method is only 'slightly lower' is not fully accurate across all metrics.

Reproducibility is limited. Key training details such as loss weights (lambda values), flow/patch dimensions, latent sizes, network depths, schedules for lambda_NI warm-up, guidance coefficients, and trust-region settings are not fully specified. No code or dataset release is mentioned, and the data generation pipeline depends on multiple external models/datasets, making reproduction difficult.

The real-world evaluation is small, covering only five objects and no quantitative pose/contact metrics. Calibration and forward-kinematics errors are acknowledged, but their effects are mostly shown qualitatively. A larger evaluation and a clear failure analysis would strengthen the practical claims.

The ablation shows that inference-time physics guidance provides only a small reconstruction gain (CD 0.036 vs. 0.033 without guidance), suggesting that most of the benefit comes from training losses and multimodal conditioning. The paper should temper the claimed importance of decoder guidance at inference.

The tactile noise ablation has an odd result: adding 5 mm tactile noise sometimes improves normal consistency and EMD over the no-noise model, which may be due to metric noise, seed variance, or an unintended regularization effect. This deserves clarification rather than being passed over.

The fixed 64^3 grid shared with the hand limits geometric fidelity for thin structures and concavities. The paper acknowledges this, but it remains a substantial limitation for manipulation tasks requiring fine geometry, and downstream refinement may not fully recover lost detail.

The DexYCB comparison with human-hand baselines is not apples-to-apples: the metrics differ from the paper's main metrics, baselines discard a large fraction of failures, and the proposed method has worse Chamfer distance than FollowMyHold (2.51 vs. 2.04) despite a much higher reconstruction rate. The comparison should be qualified more carefully.

The paper could better analyze when physical constraints actually help versus when they bias reconstruction. For example, sparse or noisy contacts could impose incorrect geometry; the current evaluation does not isolate false-positive or missed-contact scenarios sufficiently.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: amodal metric-scale object reconstruction under severe hand occlusion for robotic manipulation, where vision alone is underconstrained.

Proposes a reasonable multimodal generative pipeline that fuses egocentric RGB, proprioceptive hand pose, and multi-contact tactile signals in a shared camera-aligned SDF grid, with contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses plus inference-time guidance.

Includes simulation ablations isolating vision, proprioception, touch, physics losses, and inference guidance, which help demonstrate that the added sensing modalities contribute to geometry reconstruction.
Provides real-robot validation on a humanoid platform with a different end-effector, plus a supplementary comparison on DexYCB, showing some evidence of transfer beyond simulation.
Discusses limitations honestly, including calibration dependence, fixed 64^3 grid resolution, and shared-grid resolution loss.
weaknesses: The core method is largely incremental over existing TRELLIS/SLat/Amodal3R-style pipelines: it reuses a Structure-VAE, flow matching, and refinement modules, with the main additions being tactile/proprioceptive conditioning and physics losses. The novelty is therefore moderate rather than a fundamental advance.

The central claim of 'physically grounded' reconstruction is not quantitatively evaluated. The paper reports CD, NC, F-score, Voxel IoU, and EMD, but no interpenetration volume/rate, contact alignment error, contact normal consistency, or other physical feasibility metrics. Since physics is the main contribution, this is a serious evidentiary gap.

The experimental claims are not consistently supported by the tables. For example, in Table 1 the proposed method reports F@0.02 of 0.189 overall versus SAM3D's 0.228, so it does not improve on 'all metrics' except the least-occluded F@0.02 bin as stated. In Table 3, the real-world F@0.02 and EMD are also worse than SAM3D. This weakens the main empirical narrative.

The comparison to SAM3D is difficult to interpret: SAM3D is a much larger foundation model with more training data and is not fine-tuned on the same simulated grasp domain. Yet it already matches or exceeds the proposed method on important metrics, suggesting that the benefit of adding touch/proprioception is marginal relative to a strong vision-only baseline.

The hand latent representation is questionable: the posed hand SDF is encoded with the same Structure-VAE trained on object SDFs, then decoded to obtain the hand SDF used in the non-interpenetration loss. No evidence is provided that the object-trained VAE reconstructs hand geometry accurately, so the physics constraints may be operating on a corrupted hand field.

Real-world evaluation is limited to five YCB objects and does not report pose accuracy or physical consistency metrics. There is also no quantitative evaluation of Stage B appearance/texture despite the paper framing the method as a full reconstruction pipeline and including a texturing stage.

Reproducibility is incomplete: key hyperparameters, training schedules, compute requirements, dataset split details, and code are not sufficiently reported. Many design choices are underspecified, making it difficult to assess robustness or reproduce the results.

The paper does not compare against the most relevant tactile/vision-tactile reconstruction methods in the main experiments, and the supplementary human-hand comparison is limited. More controlled baselines with the same inputs and physical metrics are needed to substantiate the claimed advantages.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: amodal 3D reconstruction under severe hand occlusion, where vision alone is underconstrained. Integrating proprioception and multi-contact touch as geometric constraints is a natural and valuable direction for physically grounded 3D generation.

The proposed method is technically sound and well designed: a pose-aware camera-aligned SDF representation, a Structure-VAE latent space, conditional flow matching, and differentiable physics losses for contact consistency and non-interpenetration.

The use of physical constraints both as training losses and as decoder-based guidance during sampling is a principled way to encourage feasibility, and the ablation studies show that physics losses and distance-based tactile representation are important components.

The experimental evidence is relatively strong for an applied/generative systems contribution: simulation results across occlusion bins, pose-estimation metrics, real-world deployment on a humanoid robot with an unseen end-effector, robustness tests for mask/kinematic/tactile noise, and comparisons to vision-only baselines.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-articulated pipeline and sufficient implementation details in the main text and supplementary material. The limitations section is honest about calibration sensitivity, grid resolution, and frame choice.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples. The method benefits from additional sensing modalities (proprioception and touch) and a shared hand-object grid, while the vision-only baselines cannot access these signals. This is inherent to the contribution, but it means the reported improvements partly reflect additional inputs rather than a purely better generative model. A more controlled vision-only variant of the proposed architecture is helpful but does not eliminate this issue.

The metric results are mixed. In simulation, the method is better than SAM3D on CD, NC, Voxel IoU, and EMD, but worse on F@0.02; in the real-world evaluation, F@0.02 is again lower and EMD is slightly worse. The paper acknowledges some of this, but the claim of 'substantially improves completion' would be stronger with a clearer analysis of why F-score behaves differently and whether this matters for downstream manipulation.

The real-world validation is promising but limited: only five YCB objects and a small number of real trials, with performance sensitive to camera-hand calibration and forward kinematics. The cross-embodiment claim is also not fully isolated because no training end-effector is available on the real platform, as the authors note. More extensive real-world experiments and a controlled investigation of calibration/kinematic error would strengthen the transfer claim.

The fixed 64^3 grid is a meaningful bottleneck, especially because the object and hand share the same grid. Thin structures and concavities may be lost in Stage A, and although Stage B may partially recover detail, the paper does not quantitatively evaluate appearance or high-frequency geometry refinement. This limits the practical fidelity claims.

Stage B is presented as an integration step and is not central to the contribution, but the paper does not provide quantitative results for the textured/refined output. Since the abstract and introduction mention textured mesh generation, the lack of evaluation for this part leaves the end-to-end pipeline only partially validated.

Some implementation details that would aid reproducibility are underspecified or deferred, such as exact loss weights, warm-up schedules, guidance hyperparameters (beta, eta, trust-region settings), and whether code/models will be released. The supplementary material helps, but full reproducibility remains unclear.
